nameStory: Douglas' meadowfoam gets its first name from David Douglas, a Scottish botanist and explorer who collected plants along the west coast of America in the 1820s. The 'meadowfoam' part comes from how these flowers create a frothy, foam-like carpet across wet meadows in spring. Many gardeners also call it 'poached egg plant' because the white petals with bright yellow centers look exactly like a perfectly cooked poached egg!
description: Douglas' meadowfoam is a small annual wildflower that's native to California and Oregon but occasionally grown as an ornamental in New England gardens. It produces cheerful white flowers with sunny yellow centers that sit atop low, spreading plants. The flowers bloom in spring and early summer, creating a delightful cottage garden look. This low-growing plant typically stays under a foot tall and spreads naturally through self-seeding.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive white petals (usually 5) surrounding a bright golden-yellow center that looks remarkably like a poached egg - the resemblance is unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that forms loose mats or patches, rarely growing more than 6-12 inches tall but spreading outward

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, deeply divided leaves that feel slightly succulent to the touch, with narrow segments that give them a feathery appearance

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Thrives in moist to wet conditions and can tolerate heavy clay soils that would challenge many other flowering plants

habitat: In New England, Douglas' meadowfoam is extremely rare in the wild, with only 2 recorded observations. When found, it's most likely in cultivated gardens or naturalized from garden plantings. It prefers moist, poorly-drained soils and cool, wet conditions similar to its native vernal pool habitat in the Pacific Northwest.

seasonality.spring: Flowers begin blooming in late spring with their characteristic white and yellow 'poached egg' appearance. This is the best time to spot and identify this species.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming into early summer, then sets seed. Plants may start to look tired and begin dying back as summer heat increases.
seasonality.fall: Annual plants have died back, but seeds are dispersing for next year's growth. Self-seeding may occur in favorable garden conditions.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this is an annual plant. Seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring conditions.

funFact: This unassuming little flower has won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is so hardy it can self-seed and survive even when growing in a regularly mowed lawn!
confusionNotes: The 'poached egg' flower appearance is so distinctive that it's unlikely to be confused with other plants. Some white wildflowers might look similar from a distance, but the perfect yellow center surrounded by pure white petals is unique.
contextualKnowledge: Douglas' meadowfoam is extremely uncommon in New England - you're much more likely to encounter it in a specialty garden or botanical collection than in the wild. David Douglas, its namesake, was a prolific plant collector who also gave his name to the Douglas fir tree.
compareHints: Douglas' meadowfoam is the only member of its genus (Limnanthes) found in New England, making it unique in the region. Within the broader meadowfoam family, it's distinguished by its annual habit and distinctive white-and-yellow flowers. No other plants in New England share its exact 'poached egg' appearance and low, spreading growth pattern.
